bandReport.notes:
BOUNDARIES. p34 opens cleanly on item 56 with nothing above it - no item and no passage runs in from p32 (band b4, whose own report states 'p32 ends with Q55 complete, and I checked p34: it opens with Q56'). Item 56 is whole in p34-c1. At the other edge, item 80 is complete on p42-c2 (stem + all four options, closing '(d) 31') and is the last item of the 80-item paper; the '[ P.T.O.' beneath it leads to the Hindi/rough-work tail, not to more items. p42 is the last rendered page of this booklet. Nothing of mine continues beyond my pages and I have transcribed no item outside 56-80.

PASSAGE MAPPING. One directions block governs items 61-66: 'Directions for the following 6 (six) items : Read the following five passages and answer the items that follow. Your answers to these items should be based on the passages only.' printed at the head of p36-c1. FIVE passages over SIX items, distributed as: Passage-1 -> item 61 ALONE; Passage-2 -> items 62 AND 63 (this is the passage that carries two items, which is how five passages cover six items); Passage-3 -> item 64 ALONE; Passage-4 -> item 65 ALONE; Passage-5 -> item 66 ALONE. Item 63 says 'With reference to the above passage' and item 66 says 'from the above passage'; in each case I confirmed on the whole-page image that no new 'Passage-N' header stands between the item and the passage I have attached. The directions preamble itself is NOT in any context field. Every passage governing an item of mine is printed on MY OWN pages - none begins on a page I do not own - so I did not need to read a neighbouring band's page for a passage.

EXPECTED LONELY-CONTEXT WARNINGS (4). Items 61, 64, 65 and 66 each carry a context used by that item alone. These are the legitimate case the warning names - a directions block giving an item its own passage - not per-item material parked in context and not a passage lost at a band seam. This matches the same-paper precedent exactly: 2020-p2.b2 has context groups [21][22][23][24,25][26] and 2020-p2.b4 has [43][44][45,46]. My groups are [61][62,63][64][65][66]. Items 62 and 63 carry byte-identical copies of Passage-2 so they group into one consecutive set.

HASH SAFETY. Items 61 and 62 have BYTE-IDENTICAL stems ('Which one of the following is the most logical and rational inference that can be made from the above passage?'), distinguished only by their passages, which live in the hash-excluded context. No collision results because their four option sets share no text at all. The same pattern holds for items 63 and 64, which share the opening 'With reference to the above passage, the following assumptions have been made :' and an identical four-option set (1 only / 2 only / Both 1 and 2 / Neither 1 nor 2) but carry DIFFERENT numbered statement lists, which are kept in the STEM, not the context - so their stems, and therefore their hashes, stay distinct. I checked all 25 stem+option pairs in this band for collisions and found none.

CROPS. All ten column crops are clean; none is sliced, no item number is missing from the top of a c2, and no option block is cut. Every c2 crop on my pages (p34, p36, p38, p40, p42) carries a thin sliver of the neighbouring column's line-END letters down its far left margin - e.g. 'n / g / s / n' down the left edge of p34-c2 - which is the expected overlap described in the brief, not a slice. I paid particular attention to the last three pages as instructed, since the detected gutter drifts across this scan (p34 gutterX 851, p36 830, p38 857, p40 844, p42 842) and the right column is sparse on p40: p40-c2 and p42-c2 were checked item by item and both are complete. All text was read from the c1/c2 crops in the order c1-top-to-bottom then c2-top-to-bottom; the whole-page images were used only for structure - specifically to establish that Passage-2 (p36), Passage-4 (p38) and Passage-5 (p38 into p40-c1) each flow across a column or page break, after which the text itself was read from the columns.

TWO-PER-LINE OPTION LAYOUT ON p42. The last page changes its option layout: items 71, 74, 75, 76, 77, 78 and 80 print their options TWO PER LINE - '(a) ... (b) ...' on one line and '(c) ... (d) ...' on the next - rather than one per line as everywhere else in this band. Reading order within such a row is left then right, so (a) and (b) share the first line and (c) and (d) the second. Each of those seven items was re-read at 3x magnification to confirm the label-to-text pairing, because this layout is exactly where an option can be attributed to the wrong label. Item 75 is the one worth a second look: its options are printed OUT OF NUMERIC ORDER as (a) 3, (b) 4, (c) 5, (d) 2. That is verified at 3x and is what the booklet prints; it has NOT been reordered.

PRINTED DEFECT (transcribed verbatim, NOT corrected). Item 65 option (d) prints 'drinking water shortagcs in our cities' - 'shortagcs' for 'shortages'. Verified at 3x off p38-c2: the glyph after 'shorta-g' is an open 'c', clearly distinct from the closed, cross-barred 'e' in 'the' and 'reason' on the line directly above. It is a compositor's typo in the booklet and is transcribed as printed.

TYPOGRAPHY. (1) DECIMAL SEPARATOR - the booklet sets the decimal point as a raised MIDDLE DOT in its house style, and I have PRESERVED it as U+00B7 in items 69 ('46·4', '2·6'), 78 ('0·1 gm') and 80 ('4·5 m'). Each was verified at 3x; in item 69 the raised dot of '46·4' and the baseline full stop that ends the same sentence are visible side by side, so this is a distinct glyph and not a period. This follows the majority convention of the shipped Paper II corpus, including 2020-p2.b2 (7 middle dots) and the 2022-p2 and 2023-p2 bands. REPORTED FOR A HUMAN, NOT CHANGED BY ME: the other band of this same paper, 2020-p2.b4, normalised the same glyph to an ordinary full stop in 15 places (Q52's table and Q53), so 2020-p2 is internally inconsistent on this one point. That is b4's territory and I have not touched it; whoever reconciles the paper should pick one convention for both bands. No gate is affected either way. (2) Curly quotation marks and apostrophes in Passage-1, Passage-3 and Passage-5 are transcribed as straight ASCII ' and ", matching the stated convention of 2020-p2.b4. (3) The em dash in Passage-5 ('laws—assured at the outset') is preserved as U+2014, which is the corpus norm. (4) Italic emphasis is not carried into the text: the booklet sets 'most logical and rational inference' (items 61, 62), 'best reflects the critical message' (item 65), 'most logical inference' (item 66) and 'inter alia' (Passage-5) in bold italic or italic, and all are transcribed as plain text.

SUBTOPIC WARNINGS (soft, deliberate - no listed subtopic fits). Item 73 'Circles and Polygons': the item counts points of intersection of a square and a circle; the listed subtopics under 'Mensuration and Geometry' are 'Areas and Perimeters', 'Volumes and Surface Areas' and 'Lines, Angles and Triangles', and none describes it. Item 78 'Unit Conversion': the item converts between litres/kilograms and cubic millimetres/grams; no listed subtopic under 'Arithmetic Operations and Ratios' covers unit conversion. A sibling band coined 'Unit Conversion and Time Units' for a time-unit item, which I have deliberately not reused here because this item has no time component. Both are filed under listed subjects and listed chapters; only the subtopic is new.

NOT A DEFECT, RECORDED SO IT IS NOT 'FIXED' LATER. Item 77 opens 'A digit n > 3 is divisible by 3 but not divisible by 6' - 'digit', not 'number'. Verified at 3x; the word is deliberate and constrains n, so it has been left exactly as printed.

TERRITORY I DO NOT OWN - A SET THAT FAILS TO FORM, INVISIBLE TO EVERY GATE. Not my items and not changed by me; recorded because the whole-paper merge passes all four gates while still carrying it. Band b2 states in its own report that Passage-5 of the seven-item block governs BOTH item 26 (its page) and item 27 (band b3's page), and both bands duly attached that passage. But the two copies do NOT group into a set: they are 1035 characters each and differ in exactly TWO characters, the two occurrences of 'India's' in 'India's story is of' and 'India's poverty red...', where b2 wrote a straight apostrophe U+0027 and b3 wrote a curly U+2019. `assignSetLabels` keys on the whitespace-normalised, lower-cased context, which does not fold quote glyphs, so it reads them as two different passages. The merge output shows this directly: 'GATE 3b SETS: ok (4 set(s) covering 8 item(s))' with context groups [26] and [27] listed separately, and both raising lonely-context warnings. Consequence if shipped as is: Passage-5 renders TWICE, once above item 26 and once above item 27, instead of once above the pair - the exact defect the set mechanism exists to prevent - and a later correction to one copy will not mirror to the other. The fix is one character in either file, and it belongs to whoever reconciles b2 and b3, not to me. It is the same root cause as the decimal-separator divergence noted above: this paper has no single agreed convention for glyph normalisation across its bands. My own shared passage (items 62 and 63) is byte-identical in both copies and groups correctly.

questions.context: Genome editing is different from genome modification. Genome editing typically involves finding the part of a plant genome that could be changed to render it less vulnerable to disease, or resistant to certain herbicides, or to increase yields. Researchers use 'molecular scissors' to dissect the genome and repair it, which is a process that occurs naturally when plants are under attack from diseases and can throw up new mutations that enable the plant to survive future attacks. This evolutionary process can effectively be speeded up now that it is possible to examine plant genomes in detail in laboratories, and create mechanisms through which the relevant genes can be altered very precisely.
questions.stem:

2. Through genome editing, the chosen genes can be altered precisely in a manner akin to the natural process that helps plants to adapt to the environmental factors.
Which of the above assumptions is/are valid?

questions.context: In Part III of the Constitution, which assures people certain fundamental rights, Article 25 proclaims that "all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion". What people fail to notice is that this proclamation is prefixed with the words "subject to public order, morality, health and to the other provisions of this Part", which set conditions precedent for the legal protection of religious practices of any community. The closing words of this prefatory rider in Article 25 virtually constitute a subordination clause placing other fundamental rights mentioned in Part III over and above the right to religious freedom. Among those other fundamental rights is the right to equality before law and equal protection of laws—assured at the outset and elaborated in later articles to mean, inter alia, that the State shall not deny equal protection of laws to any person or group of persons on the basis of religion alone.

options.label: C
options.text: Religious freedom of the citizens is not covered under fundamental rights.

options.label: D
